title: Al-'Asr: by time
hook: by time, people are in loss, except those who believe, do good, and urge truth and patience (Surah 103)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-Humazah, the mocker who counts his money. Your line was money won't keep you. Did a joke at someone's expense rise up, and did you let it pass? Day one hundred seventy-one.

Open the screen-time report on your phone. Most people do it once, wince, and never do it again. Four hours a day. Twenty-eight hours a week. Numbers you'd never agree to if someone asked you to spend them up front. Time goes the way ice melts: not all at once, just steadily, while you're looking at something else. Today's surah is one of the shortest in the Qur'an, three lines, and it opens by swearing an oath by that very thing. Today: Al-'Asr, by time.
screen: `THE SCREEN-TIME REPORT.` → `TIME MELTS LIKE ICE.` → `AN OATH BY TIME.`

segments.voice: Here's the whole surah in Pickthall's translation: By the declining day, Lo! man is in a state of loss, Save those who believe and do good works, and exhort one another to truth and exhort one another to endurance. The first word is al-'asr. It has several meanings, and scholars keep them all. It's the late afternoon, the declining day, when the light starts to go; it's the name of the afternoon prayer, 'asr. And it's time itself, the age, an era. The root carries a sense of pressing, of squeezing something out. The afternoon is the part of the day when you feel the day being squeezed. When the Qur'an swears by something, it's asking you to look at it closely. So look at time. Then the verdict: the human being is in loss. Not some people. All of us, by default. Time is running out, every hour, like capital being spent. That's the plain math of being mortal. And then the exception. Except, and the rest of the surah is the exception. Those who believe. Those who do good. Those who urge one another to truth. Those who urge one another to patience. Tomorrow we'll look at those four closely. Today, just the first half: the oath and the loss. The surah doesn't tell you to panic. It tells you to notice. Every hour is being spent on something. By time is a question: on what?
screen: `AL-'ASR — THE DECLINING DAY, AND TIME.` · `AN OATH SAYS: LOOK CLOSELY.` · `THE HUMAN IS IN LOSS.` · `EXCEPT: THE WAY OUT OF LOSS.` · then, large: `BY TIME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Look at the clock, and notice the time. Then choose, on purpose, how you'll spend the next five minutes after this lesson. Not scrolling by default. One thing, chosen: a call to your mother, a page of something good, a walk around the block, tidying one shelf. Right now, sit and let the seconds go by without filling them. Feel them pass. They're passing either way. The bell holds the time.
Al-'Asr. Time, the declining day, and the afternoon prayer; the name of Surah one hundred three. Today's word.
Your line: by time. Spend five minutes well on purpose today. When you notice the afternoon light starting to go, let it remind you. Day one hundred seventy-one.

howItsDone: Al-'Asr is among the most memorized surahs and is often recited in the prayers; its name is shared with the afternoon prayer, and many Muslims recall it when they think about how they spend their time.

fork.setup: the surah swears by time and says the human is in loss. what comes next?
options: an exception: those who believe, do good, and urge truth and patience
a description of the end of the world
fork.reveal: the loss is the default, and the surah names the way out in the very next breath (103:3).

original.note: Arabic: time, the late afternoon; also the afternoon prayer.

trapdoor: what you thought: a surah about the afternoon.
what it means: an oath by time, a verdict that every human is losing it, and an exception.
what a scholar hears: 'asr as afternoon, era, and the afternoon prayer; the root '-s-r relates to pressing out; Pickthall renders it 'the declining day'.

sources.quoted: By the declining day, Lo! man is in a state of loss, Save those who believe and do good works, and exhort one another to truth and exhort one another to endurance.
